Who I am

Between the clinic and the community

I am a medical doctor from Burundi. My background sits at the point where clinical medicine meets community health delivery. That is where most of my work has been since 2021.

Most of my career has been about community health workers, the people who bring health services to families in villages, often far from the nearest clinic. I have trained them, supervised them in the field, built the materials they use, and worked to bring their data into national systems. Across every setting I have worked in, the model is the same: community health workers embedded in the Ministry of Health, trained through standard programmes, and placed at the frontline of care.

I always try to stay a step ahead of what global health may need next. Alongside my MSc, I deepened my data skills in R and kept learning about AI as the technology evolves. I am particularly interested in what happens behind the interface of a digital tool, not just how it is used in the field. For me, as an implementer, understanding the back end is essential to building tools that fit local health systems and have the potential to scale.

I like to understand a problem by being close to it, then find a practical way to solve it. That is the thread that connects the clinic, the community, and the technology.

My journey

From treating patients to building the systems that reach them

The short version of how my work and my interests have grown over time.

2021

Medicine, and the first pull toward community health

University of Burundi

I qualified as a medical doctor and spent about a year and a half in clinical practice: a one-year internship at Kamenge Medical Hospital, a teaching hospital in Bujumbura, followed by six months as a general practitioner at Gatumba Hospital, a remote hospital near the border with the DRC. Even as a student, I had led NCD campaigns and school health clubs and had my first experience working with the Ministry of Health. Gatumba showed me how far some people are from care, and how much responsibility falls to the health workers closest to them.

2021 to 2022

Community Health Worker Trainer

Healthy Entrepreneurs

I trained CHWs and built their training materials on smartphone use, health promotion, referral, and data collection. Some of this material was later adopted by the Ministry of Health.

2022 to 2024

Operations Manager

Healthy Entrepreneurs

I ran operations across Burundi, DRC, Kenya, Burkina Faso, and Uganda, for programmes reaching more than 5,000 CHWs. I learned to manage supply chains, budgets, teams, and Ministry of Health partnerships, and to develop funding proposals, helping mobilise more than $960K across five proposals. I was named Best Employee of the Year in 2023 and again in 2024.

2024 to 2025

Community Health Program Coordinator

Village Health Works

The period I am most proud of. I led the pilot of E-Heza, sat on the national steering committee for Burundi's Community Health Strategy 2025 to 2029, and co-developed a proposal that secured a $100K grant for local production of therapeutic food for malnourished children.

2025 to 2026

MSc Public Health and Health Promotion

Bangor University, Chevening Scholar

Field experience and programme implementation

Most of what I know, I learned in the field

In training rooms and on the paths between houses. That is where my work makes the most sense to me.

Training and supervising CHWs

I keep training active, with practice and games so people remember what to do when they are alone with a family. Then I go out and supervise real home visits. I have also trained CHWs on NCD care and community follow-up in Uganda.

Programmes with the Ministry of Health

At Healthy Entrepreneurs I helped design and run CHW programmes for malnutrition, non-communicable diseases, HIV, tuberculosis, maternal health, and integrated community case management.

NCDs at community level

I helped pilot the first integration of NCD services into the national CHW programme. NCD consultations rose by about 30%, and around 80% of chronic patients were linked to community follow-up within six months.

Supply chain and nutrition

I led the Odoo rollout that cut stockouts and delivery times by about 20%. I also led the WFP-funded Aide Alimentaire Programmee project for more than 1,000 households, and helped launch under-five malnutrition screening with Enabel.

Digital health

E-Heza: keeping a good tool alive by testing it honestly

Case study

Village Health Works planned to roll out E-Heza across a large area. E-Heza is a digital clinical decision-support tool used by community health workers during household visits, and is a Digital Public Good developed by TIP Global Health. Then the funding fell short, and the project was close to being stopped.

My role. I was a member of the national steering committee for the community health strategy, which included digitalisation. Rather than let the project end, I argued for a smaller pilot that could answer questions a large rollout could only assume: can CHWs learn and use the tool, what does training cost, and what are the practical requirements around smartphones, internet connectivity, and power? I secured VHW buy-in to move forward.

What I did. I designed the pilot from end to end, including the budget, implementation plan, CHW training, smartphone procurement, and expansion plan. I coordinated teams from Village Health Works, including CHWs, alongside TIP Global Health to contextualise E-Heza for Burundi. This included coordinating the translation of its content into Kirundi and adapting its implementation to the local health system. E-Heza had originally been developed by TIP Global Health based on experience in Rwanda. My role was to implement and contextualise the tool for the Burundian context, not to build the technology itself.

What I learned. I learned that protecting a good idea often means making it smaller, testing it honestly, and building from evidence rather than promising more than you can deliver. I also learned that good contextualisation starts by listening to the people who will use a tool. CHWs contributed to the Kirundi translation and shared their perspectives, showing me the value of involving end users in adapting digital tools to local realities.

Leadership and stakeholder engagement

Explaining community health to the people who fund it, run it, and set the rules

I would rather show this through real rooms and real partners than call myself a good communicator.

With the Ministry of Health. I have presented programme results and proposals to Ministry of Health teams, from our NCD work at community level to nutrition project results, using R visualisations to support the decisions on the table.

On national strategy. I served on the technical steering committee for Burundi's Community Health Strategy 2025 to 2029, contributing to CHW policy, financing, and digitalisation.

How I work with partners. I lead initiatives by bringing Ministry of Health technical teams, external partners, and internal colleagues around the same table, setting a clear agenda, and building the buy-in needed to move towards shared goals.

Partners I have worked with. Ministry of Health, UNICEF, WFP, Enabel, HealthNet TPO, the Gould Family Foundation, and the Community Health Impact Coalition, along with the donors behind funded proposals: the Netherlands Embassy, SNV, DKT International, and Alongside Hope.

Data and analytical skills

I can actually work with data, not just say so

I like to keep learning as global health changes. Alongside my MSc, I deepened my analysis in R through the GRAPH programme supported by the University of Geneva. Here is one example.

Malaria analysis · logistic regression

The question. Which factors are independently associated with asymptomatic malaria parasitaemia among household members of confirmed malaria patients in Abuja, Nigeria?

The finding. Living near bushes was associated with roughly twice the odds of infection, while higher education was associated with lower odds. One result stood out: uncovered water containers appeared to be associated with lower odds of infection, which was unexpected.

Why that matters. I questioned the result. Water containers were much more common in households near bushes, while proximity to bushes was itself strongly associated with infection. This overlap suggested that the apparent protective association could be influenced by confounding. For me, that is the point of data work: reading a result carefully, questioning what might be behind it, and being honest about what the data can and cannot show.

# Multivariable logistic regression
multiv <- glm(malaria_parasitaemia ~ age_group + sex +
              education + bushes + llin_night + house_type +
              index_case + water_receptacles,
              family = binomial, data = nigeria_malaria)

tidy(multiv, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

AI applied to health

Support for health workers at the moment they need it

My interest in AI grew out of my digital health work. CHWs make important decisions during home visits, often alone, with little support right when they need it.

The idea: CHW Companion

An AI decision-support concept for CHWs in rural areas. A health worker sends a voice note in their own language through WhatsApp, a channel they already use, and gets clear guidance based on trusted protocols from the WHO, Africa CDC, and national guidelines. It flags danger signs for referral and keeps no identifiable patient data.

My contribution

This is a concept I designed, and I have built the technical pipelines behind it. It is not deployed yet, and I am looking for partners and funding to pilot it. To be precise: this is something I am building and testing, not a tool already running in the field.

The technology

A large language model with retrieval-augmented generation, so answers are grounded in real protocols rather than invented, together with speech-to-text so health workers can speak instead of type.

What I learned, and next

Building it gave me a view of what happens behind the interface, not just how a tool is used. It connects directly to my dissertation on AI in African primary care. The next step is to test it properly and build it to scale, rather than leave it as another pilot.
